findings.title: Device-limit check is a non-atomic check-then-act, allowing the limit to be exceeded under concurrent load
findings.body: In CreateOrUpdateDevice, the code first calls CountDevices to read the current count, then decides whether to insert a new device or fall back to updateDevice. There is no transaction, row lock, or unique-constraint-based enforcement tying the count check to the subsequent insert. Under concurrent anonymous requests (which is the normal case for this feature), multiple goroutines can simultaneously read a count that is below the limit and all proceed to insert new devices, allowing the configured anonymousDeviceLimit to be exceeded by an arbitrary margin. This defeats the purpose of the feature under real traffic.

findings.title: Anonymous device tagging changed from async fire-and-forget to a synchronous, blocking call inside Authenticate, adding DB latency/risk to every anonymous request
findings.body: Previously TagDevice was invoked in a separate goroutine with its own timeout context and panic recovery, so DB latency or panics in the tagging path could not affect the anonymous authentication request. This PR removes that goroutine and panic-recovery wrapper and calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...) synchronously in Authenticate. This is required to make ErrDeviceLimitReached able to block authentication, but it also means every anonymous request (at least until the device is cached) now blocks on a DB round-trip (and, when the device limit is enabled, an additional CountDevices query) as part of the authentication hot path, and any panic inside TagDevice is no longer isolated from the request. This is a potential latency/availability regression for installs with many anonymous users.

findings.title: New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is not documented anywhere
findings.body: setting.go adds a new ini key `device_limit` under the `[auth.anonymous]` section (cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)), but no changes were made to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the configuration documentation pages describing this new option, its default value (0 = unlimited), or its effect. Administrators have no way to discover this new, user-facing configuration knob.

findings.title: No test covers that Authenticate rejects anonymous login once the device limit is exceeded
findings.body: The new behavior in Authenticate propagates anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached from TagDevice back to the authn broker, effectively denying anonymous authentication once the device limit is reached. Only anonstore/database_test.go (TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit) tests the lower-level store behavior; there is no test exercising Anonymous.Authenticate or the end-to-end AnonDeviceService.TagDevice flow to confirm the error is correctly surfaced/handled (vs. other, non-limit errors which should be swallowed). This leaves the primary new user-facing behavior of the feature (anonymous users get rejected beyond the device limit) without direct test coverage.

findings.title: Device-activity window constant duplicated across packages risks silent drift
findings.body: anonymousDeviceExpiration (30 days) is now defined independently in pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go and pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/api/api.go, while pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go already has its own separate `thirtyDays` constant with the same value used for usage-stat counting. These three constants must be kept in sync by hand across files/packages; if one is changed (e.g., to adjust the retention/activity window) without updating the others, the device-limit count, the /api/anonymous/devices listing window, and the usage-stat count will become inconsistent with each other.

findings.title: Anonymous device limit value is exposed to unauthenticated users via frontend settings
findings.body: AnonymousDeviceLimit is added to FrontendSettingsDTO and populated unconditionally from hs.Cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit in getFrontendSettings, which is served by GetFrontendSettings without requiring authentication (it is accessible to anonymous users since this endpoint powers anonymous access itself). This leaks an operational/security-relevant configuration value (the device cap) to any unauthenticated caller, which could help an attacker determine how close the deployment is to its device limit or tune an attack to exhaust it.
